subject: Reproductive
subtopic: Adnexal torsion and pelvic organ prolapse
vignette: A 24-year-old woman develops sudden severe right lower-quadrant pain with nausea and vomiting. Pelvic examination reveals a tender right adnexal mass, and ultrasound shows an enlarged ovary with reduced blood flow. She is taken urgently to the operating room.
question: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation_correct: Adnexal torsion is the twisting of the ovary and fallopian tube around the infundibulopelvic and ovarian ligaments, often associated with an ovarian mass or cyst. It produces acute pelvic pain, an adnexal mass, and nausea/vomiting, and decreased blood flow on ultrasound supports the diagnosis. It is a surgical emergency because untreated torsion leads to ovarian necrosis.

explanation_incorrect.A: A ruptured ectopic pregnancy would typically present with amenorrhea, vaginal bleeding, and a positive hCG rather than an ischemic adnexal mass with reduced flow.
explanation_incorrect.B: Appendicitis causes periumbilical pain migrating to the right lower quadrant with anorexia and fever; it does not produce a tender adnexal mass or reduced ovarian blood flow.
explanation_incorrect.D: Simple ovarian cyst rupture causes sudden pain but usually no persistent adnexal mass, and it lacks the arterial/venous flow compromise seen here.
explanation_incorrect.E: Pelvic inflammatory disease presents with fever, vaginal discharge, and cervical motion tenderness, usually bilaterally, rather than an acute unilateral ischemic adnexal mass.

educationalObjective: Adnexal torsion presents with acute pelvic pain, an adnexal mass, and nausea/vomiting and is a surgical emergency.

subject: Reproductive
subtopic: Adnexal torsion and pelvic organ prolapse
vignette: A 31-year-old woman with a known left ovarian cyst develops abrupt pelvic pain. At surgery the left adnexa is twisted; the ovary is edematous and hemorrhagic but not yet frankly necrotic. The surgeon explains the sequence of vascular compromise that produced these findings.
question: Which of the following best describes the vascular sequence in adnexal torsion?

options.text: Venous and lymphatic outflow is obstructed while arterial inflow continues, causing edema before arterial inflow ceases and necrosis develops
Arterial inflow is blocked first, producing instantaneous necrosis without an edematous phase
Lymphatic outflow increases, draining interstitial fluid and preventing ovarian swelling
Venous outflow remains patent while arterial inflow increases, causing hemorrhage without edema
Arterial and venous flow stop simultaneously, so the ovary becomes necrotic immediately

explanation_correct: Twisting compresses the ovarian vessels, blocking lymphatic and venous outflow first. Because arterial perfusion continues through the higher-pressure arteries, the ovary becomes edematous and congested; with persistent torsion, arterial inflow is eventually blocked completely, leading to necrosis and local hemorrhage. This reversible early stage is why prompt detorsion can salvage the ovary.

explanation_incorrect.B: Arterial inflow persists initially because arteries are thicker and higher pressure; necrosis is a late event, not instantaneous.
explanation_incorrect.C: Lymphatic outflow is blocked by the torsion, not increased, so interstitial fluid accumulates and the ovary swells.
explanation_incorrect.D: Venous and lymphatic outflow are impaired rather than preserved; the combination of continued arterial inflow and blocked outflow produces edema, not hemorrhage alone.
explanation_incorrect.E: Flow does not cease simultaneously; there is an early edematous, potentially reversible phase before irreversible necrosis, which is the basis for emergent surgery.

educationalObjective: In torsion, venous/lymphatic outflow is blocked while arterial inflow persists, causing edema before arterial compromise and necrosis.

subject: Reproductive
subtopic: Adnexal torsion and pelvic organ prolapse
vignette: During surgical detorsion, the surgeon observes the ovary and fallopian tube rotating as a unit around their supporting attachments. The ovarian vessels whose compression caused the congestion travel within one of the ligaments forming this axis of rotation.
question: Around which of the following structures does the ovary and fallopian tube twist in adnexal torsion?
explanation_correct: Adnexal torsion is defined as twisting of the ovary and fallopian tube around the infundibulopelvic (suspensory) and ovarian (utero-ovarian) ligaments. The ovarian vessels travel within the infundibulopelvic ligament, and their compression blocks venous and lymphatic drainage. This anatomic axis explains both the congestion and the potential for necrosis.

explanation_incorrect.A: The round ligament traverses the inguinal canal and the broad ligament is a peritoneal fold; neither forms the axis around which the adnexa twist.
explanation_incorrect.B: The cardinal and uterosacral ligaments support the cervix and vaginal apex and are not part of the ovarian torsion axis.
explanation_incorrect.C: The utero-ovarian (ovarian) ligament is one component of the axis, but torsion also involves the infundibulopelvic ligament carrying the ovarian vessels, so it is not the utero-ovarian ligament alone.
explanation_incorrect.E: Uterosacral and cardinal ligaments are cervical support structures and do not surround or suspend the ovary and tube.

educationalObjective: The ovary and fallopian tube twist around the infundibulopelvic and ovarian ligaments in adnexal torsion.

subject: Reproductive
subtopic: Adnexal torsion and pelvic organ prolapse
vignette: A 58-year-old woman who has had four vaginal deliveries reports pelvic pressure, a bulging sensation, and urinary frequency. Examination shows the bladder bulging into the anterior vaginal wall. She is told she has pelvic organ prolapse and asks which form is most common.
question: Which of the following is the most common type of pelvic organ prolapse?
explanation_correct: Anterior compartment prolapse, in which the bladder herniates into the anterior vaginal wall (cystocele), is the most common type of pelvic organ prolapse. Risk factors include multiparity, increasing age, and obesity, and symptoms include pelvic pressure, bulging, urinary frequency, constipation, and sexual dysfunction.

explanation_incorrect.A: A rectocele is a posterior compartment prolapse of the rectum into the posterior vaginal wall and is less common than cystocele.
explanation_incorrect.B: An enterocele is a posterior compartment prolapse of small bowel into the vaginal vault and is less common than anterior prolapse.
explanation_incorrect.C: Apical prolapse involves descent of the uterus, cervix, or vaginal vault and is less common than isolated anterior compartment prolapse.
explanation_incorrect.D: Uterine procidentia involves all three compartments and represents advanced, not the most common isolated, prolapse.

educationalObjective: Cystocele (anterior compartment/bladder prolapse) is the most common type of pelvic organ prolapse.

subject: Reproductive
subtopic: Adnexal torsion and pelvic organ prolapse
vignette: A 72-year-old woman has a large mass protruding beyond the vaginal introitus. Evaluation demonstrates herniation of the bladder into the anterior wall, of the rectum into the posterior wall, and complete descent of the uterus and cervix to the vaginal vault.
question: Which of the following terms best describes this finding?
explanation_correct: Uterine procidentia is complete prolapse involving all three compartments: anterior (bladder/cystocele), posterior (rectum/rectocele), and apical (uterus, cervix, and vaginal vault). It is the most advanced form of pelvic organ prolapse and is associated with multiparity, increasing age, and obesity.

explanation_incorrect.A: An isolated cystocele involves only the anterior compartment and would not include rectal herniation or descent of the uterus and cervix.
explanation_incorrect.C: An isolated rectocele involves only the posterior compartment and would not include bladder herniation or apical descent.
explanation_incorrect.D: An enterocele is a posterior compartment prolapse of small bowel only, not a three-compartment prolapse.
explanation_incorrect.E: Apical prolapse alone involves the uterus, cervix, or vaginal vault but spares the anterior and posterior compartments described here.

educationalObjective: Uterine procidentia is herniation involving all three prolapse compartments: anterior, posterior, and apical.
